title: Engineering with AI Assistants
oneLiner: Use AI coding tools to go faster without becoming a proxy for them: understand and verify what they write, review diffs critically, test, debug when they are wrong, and keep secrets out.
keyTakeaway: You are responsible for every line you commit, whoever typed it. Use assistants for what they are good at (boilerplate, unfamiliar APIs, first drafts, explaining code, writing tests), give them context and small tasks, and then read the diff as a reviewer would: can you explain each line, does it do what was asked and nothing else, do the tests prove it? Never paste secrets or customer data into a tool your company hasn't approved, and write it yourself when you are learning, when the code is security-critical, or when explaining the task would take longer than doing it.
explanation:
AI coding assistants now range from autocomplete in the editor to chat in the IDE to agents that read the repository, edit files and run commands on their own. Used well they remove a lot of tedium. Used badly they produce code that nobody on the team understands, and an engineer whose real job has become copying error messages into a chat box. The aim of this lesson is the first without the second. For how the models themselves work and fail, see the AI & Machine Learning section, especially Using LLMs Well and Risks and Limits.

What they are good at: boilerplate and repetitive edits (a DTO and its mapping, a migration, the fifth similar endpoint), first drafts in a language or library you know less well, translating between languages, explaining a confusing piece of code or an error message, writing tests for behaviour you describe, regular expressions and shell one-liners (which you then test), and searching a large codebase for where something happens. What they are weak at: anything that depends on context they don't have (your business rules, the incident last month, why that odd check exists), APIs newer than their training data, which they will confidently invent, subtle concurrency and security issues, and knowing when they are wrong. They can produce code that compiles, looks idiomatic and is wrong in a way a quick read misses.

Working effectively. Give the assistant what a new colleague would need: the relevant files, the constraints, the conventions, an example of the style you want. Ask for small, reviewable steps rather than a whole feature at once. Ask it to explain its plan before it writes code, and to say what it is unsure about. When an agent is working on its own, give it a way to check its work (tests it can run, a build that must pass) and keep the changes on a branch you review before merging.

Reviewing generated code is the core skill, and it is the same skill as reviewing a colleague's pull request, with less trust. Read the whole diff, not the summary. For every line ask: do I understand what this does and why it is needed? Check that each API it calls exists and behaves as assumed (open the docs; invented methods and wrong parameter orders are common). Look for what is missing: error handling, input validation, the empty, null and boundary cases, cancellation and timeouts, logging of sensitive data. Look for things you didn't ask for: unrelated refactors, new dependencies (check that a suggested package really exists and is the one you think, because attackers register packages under names that models tend to invent), weakened tests, a disabled check. If you can't explain a line to a reviewer, you are not ready to commit it.

Testing is how you verify rather than hope. Write or ask for tests that pin down the behaviour, including edge cases, and read them as carefully as the code: a generated test that asserts whatever the code currently returns proves nothing. Watch for an assistant that makes a failing test pass by changing the test. Run the code; a plausible answer isn't a working one.

When the AI is wrong, and it will be, debugging is still your job. Don't loop by pasting the same error back and accepting each new guess; after two failed attempts, stop and debug normally: reproduce the problem, read the actual error and stack trace, form a hypothesis, check it with a debugger or a log line, and narrow it down. Often the assistant was missing one fact you can supply once you have found it. If you don't understand the code well enough to debug it, that is the signal that you accepted too much at once.

Security and privacy. Anything you paste into a tool may leave your machine. Use only tools your organisation has approved for its code, and never paste secrets (API keys, connection strings, passwords, tokens, private keys) or customer and personal data. If a secret does end up in a prompt, a commit or a log, treat it as leaked: rotate it, don't just delete the message. Review generated code for the usual vulnerabilities (string-built SQL, missing authorisation checks, unescaped output, secrets in code) with extra care, because the model learned from plenty of insecure examples. Agents that run commands need limits: no production credentials, review before anything destructive, and a sandbox where possible. Content an agent reads (a web page, an issue, a file) can contain instructions aimed at it, which is prompt injection.

When to write it yourself: when you are learning (the struggle is how the skill forms, and interviews have no assistant), when the code is security- or money-critical and every line needs deliberate thought, when the task is small enough that explaining it takes longer than typing it, and when you have already corrected the assistant twice. A good habit is to sketch the approach yourself first, then let the tool help with the typing.

Two things are easy to lose. Understanding: if a teammate asks why the code does something, "the AI wrote it" is not an answer, and ownership includes being able to maintain it at 2 a.m. Judgement: the assistant can suggest designs, but choosing between them, and knowing when none is right, is the engineer's job. Practise without the tools regularly so the fundamentals stay yours.

Part 1 is a code review of an AI-generated change with planted problems to find. Part 2 is a set of everyday situations: pick what you would do and compare with the reasoning.
